nameStory: The ivy-leaved morning-glory gets its name from its distinctive three-lobed leaves that look remarkably similar to English ivy leaves. Like other morning-glories, its trumpet-shaped flowers open in the early morning hours, greeting the dawn with their colorful display. The 'morning-glory' name captures this daily ritual of flowers unfurling as the sun rises.
description: Ivy-leaved morning-glory is a climbing vine that twists and winds its way up fences, poles, and other plants using its flexible stems. This annual vine can grow several feet long in a single season, covering surfaces with heart-shaped leaves that are typically divided into three pointed lobes. From summer through late fall, it produces beautiful trumpet-shaped flowers that are blue to rose-purple with bright white throats. Originally from tropical America, this adaptable vine has made itself at home across much of North America.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with three distinct pointed lobes, resembling ivy leaves. The leaves feel smooth and thin, arranged alternately along the twining stem. Occasionally you might find five-lobed or unlobed leaves on the same plant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Trumpet-shaped flowers about 1-2 inches across, blue to rose-purple with a crisp white throat inside. Flowers appear in small clusters of 1-3 blooms and have a delicate, papery texture when you gently touch the petals.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Vigorous twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around supports. The stems feel smooth and slightly succulent, with a green color that may have reddish tinges.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, papery capsules that split open to reveal dark brown to black seeds. The capsules make a soft rustling sound when dry and are surrounded by sepals with long, curved-back tips.

habitat: Look for ivy-leaved morning-glory in disturbed areas like roadsides, field edges, gardens, and waste places throughout New England. It thrives in full sun and well-drained soils, often climbing on fences, utility poles, or scrambling over other vegetation. This adaptable vine tolerates poor soils and drought once established.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, and young vines begin their rapid growth with the first heart-shaped leaves appearing.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season begins with trumpet flowers opening in early morning hours and often closing by midday in hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues until first frost, with seed capsules forming and ripening to brown. The entire plant dies back with cold weather.
seasonality.winter: Only dried seed capsules remain, often persisting on dead stems and releasing seeds for next year's growth.

funFact: Morning-glory flowers are nature's alarm clocks - they typically open around 6 AM and close by noon on hot days, but on cool, cloudy days they might stay open all day long, as if they're hitting the snooze button!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common morning-glory, but ivy-leaved morning-glory has distinctly three-lobed leaves while common morning-glory has heart-shaped leaves that are usually unlobed. Memory trick: 'Ivy-leaved has lobes like ivy leaves.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beauty, ivy-leaved morning-glory can be quite aggressive in gardens and is sometimes considered weedy. The seeds remain viable in soil for many years, so even after removing the vines, new plants may continue to appear for several seasons.
compareHints: Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves. The white throat contrasting with blue-purple petals is also distinctive, as many relatives have more uniformly colored flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
